title: Technical deep dive: model architecture tuning (Llama/Mistral/Qwen, MoE, RoPE)

meeting_header: Date: 2026-12-15 | Time: 15:00 UTC | Duration: 52m | Attendees: Alex Chen, Samira Patel, Diego Ramos (Redwood) - Mark Rivera, Priya Singh, Joan Lee, Evan Kline (HelixAI)
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: thanks everyone for joining, we'll focus on architecture-specific tuning for Llama, Mistral and Qwen, and also touch on MoE and RoPE scaling.  Priya can you confirm the main success criteria?
[00:18] Priya Singh: yeah, low single-request latency for our chat product, plus keeping cost per 1k tokens under our current baseline. we also need deterministic behavior for eval sets.
[00:32] Samira Patel: perfect. quick agenda: latency/throughput baseline, kv cache strategy, batching and continous batching tuning, quantization profiles, then VPC/on-prem gotchas. Diego will chime in on infra.
[00:47] Mark Rivera: we'll likely deploy in our private cluster (8xA100) behind a VPC, so things like kernel choices and NUMA binding matter.
[00:58] Diego Ramos: noted, we saw high tail latency when slotting multiple models on the same machine, suspected interference in CUDA streams and GPU memory arena.
[01:12] Samira Patel: for Llama family the common trick is to adjust RoPE scaling when you use longer context; mismatch in positional encoding can cause hallucination drift and perplexity spikes - you probably need progressive scaling if you're fine-tuning or using longer sequences than original pretrain.
[01:34] Evan Kline: wait, progressive scaling? so we rescale RoPE factors at runtime? how stable is that?
[01:41] Samira Patel: it's stable if you bake it into the tokenizer/serving config - we apply a linear rescale based on max_seq_len; for Mistral it's trickier because some weights assume absolute positions, so we recommend a small fine-tune or adapter when you change sequence length significantly.
[01:58] Priya Singh: ok, so for Qwen any special notes?
[02:02] Samira Patel: Qwen uses a slightly different rotary implementation and tends to be more sensitive to quant noise. when you combine 4-bit quant and RoPE rescaling you can see token shifts; we recommend keeping Qwen at 8-bit quant for critical paths or using per-channel quant for certain attention kernels.
[02:22] Mark Rivera: on MoE models - we're evaluating them for higher-quality next-token sampling, but worried about routing overhead. what's the cost?
[02:29] Alex Chen: good question. MoE routing cost is twofold: the extra compute when activating experts, and the memory+communication overhead when you redistribute tokens across devices. in small batch, single-request setups the routing decision latency dominates.
[02:45] Diego Ramos: in our tests with a 16-expert model we saw ~30-50% extra tail latency for single-stream inference because of the scatter-gather. batching helps amortize it.
[02:56] Samira Patel: exactly - for MoE, we recommend dedicated pools with larger micro-batches and pipeline parallelism to amortize routing. Redwood's smart routing can fallback to dense variants if the pool is underutilized to meet SLOs.
[03:14] Priya Singh: how about KV cache - we want prefix caching for chat history to reduce tokens processed per request. any gotchas?
[03:21] Samira Patel: KV cache is very effective, but you need to tune cache granularity: full-turn vs token-level. token-level cache gives best perf but increases memory. also cold-starts matter - we saw 10-15% latency spikes on cold prefixes.
[03:38] Alex Chen: one trick is to persist warmed KV caches for active sessions on a fast shared memory (NVMe-backed mmap or on-GPU pinned memory) and have cache affinity to avoid reloading. Redwood supports persistent KV across requests in dedicated pools.
[03:54] Evan Kline: any advice on eviction policy? we have many short-lived sessions.
[03:58] Samira Patel: LRU with TTL tuned to session behavior usually works, or size-based eviction where you compress older KV with lossy quantization. also consider prefix summarization - compress older context into a short summary to keep cache small.
[04:15] Mark Rivera: batching - our users expect sub-200ms p95. batching usually increases throughput but hurts p95. how do you tune?
[04:23] Diego Ramos: continuous batching with time budget is key. set a micro-batch delay of 5-10ms to collect tokens, then flush. Redwood's runtime can set per-route latency budgets and adaptive batch sizes based on current load.
[04:39] Samira Patel: also dynamic batching by sequence length helps. group similar-length requests to reduce padding overhead. and use attention kernel selection tuned to sequence distribution.
[04:52] Priya Singh: quantization - curious about 4-bit; we've seen big model size savings but worried about quality.
[04:59] Samira Patel: 4-bit (PTQ) can work for many Mistral variants, but for Qwen and some Llama checkpoints you may see consistent degradation in completion coherence. we recommend mixed strategy: run 4-bit for feed-forward layers and 8-bit for attention, or use GPTQ with per-channel scales. Redwood's compiled kernels include optimized 4-bit matmul but with fallback to 8-bit for attention when accuracy drop detected.
[05:25] Alex Chen: we should run a short A/B on your eval set - Samira can provide suggested quant profiles.
[05:31] Samira Patel: yes, will add to action items.
[05:34] Mark Rivera: VPC/on-prem - encryption and KMS. we need to ensure model weights never leave our VPC, and audit logs are centrally stored. any blockers with Redwood Private?
[05:45] Diego Ramos: Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and on-prem package; but in previous installs customers had to adjust their kube-device-plugin and set CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES explicitly to avoid cross-tenant visibility. also HSM integration sometimes needs custom drivers.
[06:02] Samira Patel: important note: if you use persistent KV on shared disks, ensure those volumes are encrypted with your key; Redwood can configure mount options to satisfy that.
[06:11] Priya Singh: how about rolling upgrades and canaries for model weights? we want zero-downtime and fast rollback if quality regresses.
[06:19] Alex Chen: Redwood supports canary rollouts by traffic split and automatic fallback. for heavy models we suggest a staged rollout: 5% traffic, then 25%, then 100% with automated eval checks on your prompt set.
[06:33] Evan Kline: what about rope scaling affecting eval metrics mid-rollout?
[06:37] Samira Patel: run the rollout with the same RoPE config and if you must change RoPE scale, do it in the canary first and compare token-level metrics - keep a metric for token-shift or perplexity delta.
[06:50] Mark Rivera: are there any recommended kernel/driver versions for A100s?
[06:54] Diego Ramos: Nvidia 535+ driver and CUDA 12.x are stable for our kernels; use cuBLASLt optimized matmul and make sure to pin NUMA for multi-GPU; avoid MPS for isolated latency-sensitive workloads - MPS can improve throughput but may increase jitter.
[07:12] Alex Chen: ok let's talk concrete next steps - we'll send the benchmark plan, Samira will propose quant profiles, and you (HelixAI) will provide access for a short run.
[07:22] Priya Singh: timeline works. any competitors or other tech we should watch for?
[07:27] Samira Patel: Anthropic's approach to attention kernels is interesting but not production-proven on private clusters; OpenAI's hosted managed endpoints avoid this complexity but we think you want control.
[07:39] Mark Rivera: noted. thanks.
[07:43] Alex Chen: quick recap: Redwood shares spreadsheet and recommended settings; HelixAI runs benchmarks and returns logs; schedule canary week of 2026-12-28.
[07:53] Evan Kline: thanks all.
[07:56] [crosstalk] end of recording
